questions.q: State the precise mathematical condition for a function \( f \) to be continuous at \( x = c \) using left-hand limit, right-hand limit, and function value.
questions.a: Correct answer: \( \lim_{x \to c^-} f(x) = \lim_{x \to c^+} f(x) = f(c) \). All three must exist as finite real numbers and be equal. A wrong answer that only says “LHL = RHL” reveals the student forgets to check \( f(c) \) — a classic error where the function has a removable discontinuity (hole) but the limits match.

questions.q: Explain why the function \( f(x) = \begin{cases} x+1, & x < 2 \\ 4, & x = 2 \\ x^2, & x > 2 \end{cases} \) is discontinuous at \( x = 2 \), even though the left-hand and right-hand limits are equal.
questions.a: At \( x = 2 \): LHL = \( \lim_{x \to 2^-} (x+1) = 3 \), RHL = \( \lim_{x \to 2^+} x^2 = 4 \). The limits are NOT equal (3 ≠ 4), so the function is discontinuous. A student who claims LHL = RHL = 3 has incorrectly used the left‑piece for the right-hand limit, revealing confusion about which piece applies on which side of the boundary.

questions.q: For \( f(x) = \begin{cases} 2x + 3, & x \le 1 \\ ax^2 + 1, & x > 1 \end{cases} \), find the value of \( a \) that makes \( f \) continuous at \( x = 1 \).
questions.a:
Step 1: \( f(1) = 2(1) + 3 = 5 \) (using the first piece because \( x \le 1 \)).  
Step 2: LHL = \( \lim_{x \to 1^-} (2x+3) = 5 \).  
Step 3: RHL = \( \lim_{x \to 1^+} (ax^2+1) = a(1)^2 + 1 = a + 1 \).  
Step 4: For continuity, LHL = RHL = \( f(1) \) ⇒ \( 5 = a + 1 \) ⇒ \( a = 4 \).  
A wrong answer \( a = 5 \) comes from setting \( a+1 = 5 \) but mistakenly using \( f(1) = 6 \) or mis‑evaluating the limit.

questions.q: Compare the continuity at \( x = 0 \) of \( f(x) = |x| \) and \( g(x) = \begin{cases} -1, & x < 0 \\ 1, & x \ge 0 \end{cases} \). Both are piecewise; why is one continuous and the other not?
questions.a:
For \( f(x) = |x| \): LHL = \( \lim_{x \to 0^-} (-x) = 0 \), RHL = \( \lim_{x \to 0^+} x = 0 \), \( f(0) = 0 \) → all equal, continuous.  
For \( g(x) \): LHL = \( \lim_{x \to 0^-} (-1) = -1 \), RHL = \( \lim_{x \to 0^+} 1 = 1 \), \( g(0) = 1 \) → LHL ≠ RHL, discontinuous.  
A student who says both are continuous because they are “defined everywhere” misses that continuity requires the limits to match the value, not just existence of definition.

questions.q: A student claims: “\( f(x) = \frac{x^2 - 4}{x - 2} \) is continuous at \( x = 2 \) because the limit as \( x \to 2 \) is 4.” Evaluate this claim.
questions.a: The claim is FALSE. \( f(2) \) is undefined (division by zero). Even though \( \lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 2} (x+2) = 4 \), the function value does not exist. Continuity requires \( f(c) \) to exist and equal the limit. The student’s error is ignoring the domain condition — a removable discontinuity (hole) at \( x = 2 \).

questions.q: Construct a piecewise function \( h(x) \) with two different polynomial pieces that is continuous at \( x = 3 \) and satisfies \( h(3) = 7 \). Write the function and verify continuity.
questions.a:
Example: \( h(x) = \begin{cases} x + 4, & x \le 3 \\ 2x + 1, & x > 3 \end{cases} \).  
Check: \( h(3) = 3+4 = 7 \); LHL = \( \lim_{x \to 3^-} (x+4) = 7 \); RHL = \( \lim_{x \to 3^+} (2x+1) = 7 \). All equal → continuous.  
A poor answer gives pieces that don’t meet at \( (3,7) \) or uses non‑polynomial pieces, showing inability to reverse‑engineer the condition.
